run.label: Changed-Pages Pass · At an Event · CloudShell
run.standfirst: Only the pages changed since the last tested run are walked, each in full, in CloudShell, against the Workshop Studio environment that run left standing.
run.questionTitle: Do the pages that changed still work?
run.question:
Set at run start: the baseline commit and the list of changed pages.

Proves those pages and nothing else — no other page and no infrastructure.

phases.step: Step 1 — Ask the agent (no sign-in)
phases.does: You have the real web address of your own deployment's chat page, rather than a hostname typed from somewhere else.
phases.cmd: source infrastructure/.acme-state && echo "Ask page: https://${NIP_FQDN_BANKING}/ask"
phases.expected: Prints "Ask page: https://<your banking FQDN>/ask".
phases.trackNote: A changed-pages board lists only the pages changed since the last tested run, in workshop order, each run in full. These seven are the pages this branch changes.

phases.step: Step 1 — Ask the agent (no sign-in)
phases.sub: Open the ask page and ask a question
phases.does: Anyone can get a real answer grounded in the company documents without logging in, and the agent had none of the credentials it used until the moment you asked.
phases.cmd:
Open the printed https://<banking FQDN>/ask URL in your browser.
Check for the lock icon in the address bar.
Without signing in, ask: "Summarize the employee PTO policy, including accrual by tenure."
phases.expected: A lock icon (Let's Encrypt cert) and a Knowledge-Base-grounded answer: PTO accrual of 15 days at 0–2 years, 20 at 2–5, 25 at 5+. A "Your connection is not private" warning is a regression.

phases.step: Step 2 — Inspect the credential metadata (CLI)
phases.does: You can reach the agent's own API directly instead of only the chat page, which is where the credential detail is visible.
phases.cmd: kubectl port-forward -n uc1 svc/uc1-agent-svc 8080:80

phases.step: Step 2 — Inspect the credential metadata (CLI)
phases.sub: Send the SQL-shaped question from a second terminal
phases.does: The pod proved who it was to Vault using its Kubernetes identity rather than a stored key, was handed a database credential good for fifteen minutes, and hands you back that credential's lease id to carry into the next step.
phases.cmd:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "Run a SQL query to list any tables in the database."}' \
  | jq '{answer: .answer, credential_metadata: .credential_metadata}'
phases.expected: JSON with an answer plus credential_metadata: vault_authenticated true, vault_role uc1, and one lease for database/creds/uc1-readonly with a lease_id and ttl_seconds 900.

phases.step: Step 3 — Observe credential issuance in the Vault audit log
phases.does: The answer somebody read can be tied back to the exact credential Vault handed out for it, and to the ServiceAccount that asked — the same lease id appears on both sides.
phases.cmd:
kubectl logs -n vault -l app.kubernetes.io/name=vault --since=15m --tail=-1 \
  | jq -c 'select(.type=="response" and .request.path=="database/creds/uc1-readonly")
           | {time, path: .request.path,
              display_name: .auth.display_name,
              lease_id: .response.secret.lease_id}' \
  | tail -1
phases.expected: One JSON line: time, path database/creds/uc1-readonly, display_name kubernetes-uc1-uc1-retriever-sa, and the same lease_id Step 2 printed.

phases.step: Step 4 — ENFC-01 enforcement test (the thing that must NOT happen)
phases.does: The read-only agent cannot get the refund-writing credentials even when it asks with its own genuine identity — Vault refuses, and the refusal is the pass.
phases.cmd:
kubectl exec -n uc1 deploy/uc1-agent -- python3 -c '
from app.agent import _vault
_vault.login()
try:
    _vault.client.read("database/creds/uc3-refund-writer")
    print("BREACH — UC1 obtained UC3 write credentials")
except Exception as e:
    print("DENIED (expected):", type(e).__name__)
'
phases.expected: DENIED (expected): Forbidden

phases.step: Step 5 — Run verify-uc1.sh
phases.does: Everything claimed on this page is checked in one command, including the parts there is never time to demonstrate by hand, and a failure tells you how to fix it.
phases.cmd: bash infrastructure/scripts/verify-uc1.sh
phases.expected: Ten PASS lines (pod, ServiceAccount, Vault role, JIT DB creds, JIT STS creds, /health, ENFC-01, Agent Registry, audit device, /query end-to-end) then "✓ 10 check(s) passed"; a failure prints a copy-paste Fix hint.

phases.step: Platform/Security Track — Vault lease lifecycle: issuance, TTL, auto-revocation
phases.does: You can watch the database credential exist right after a query and then vanish on its own fifteen minutes later, with no password left to rotate.
phases.expected: The list contains the last segment of the lease_id that Step 2 returned. Run it again after 15 minutes and that segment is gone, because Vault has revoked the lease and dropped the Postgres role.

phases.trackLabel: Phase 3 — Use Case 2: OAuth Personalized Read-Only
phases.step: Step 1 — Get the Banking UI URL
phases.does: You have the real address of your own banking site, read back from the deployment instead of typed from a guess.
phases.cmd: echo "https://$(grep '^NIP_FQDN_BANKING=' infrastructure/.acme-state | cut -d= -f2)/"

phases.step: Step 2 — Sign in at the IVIA login page
phases.does: Your password is only ever typed on the identity provider's page — the banking app never sees it and still ends up knowing who you are.
phases.cmd: Open the Banking UI URL in a fresh incognito / private window. The browser is redirected to the IVIA WebSEAL login page. Enter username `oscar` and password `WorkshopUser1!`, then click **Login**. This window is your **oscar window**. Leave it open.
phases.expected: WebSEAL redirects back through /isvaop/oauth2/authorize to the Banking UI's /callback?code=... and you land on /dashboard.

phases.step: Step 3 — Inspect the Banking UI logs
phases.does: The banking app took delivery of a token it never minted and cannot forge — nothing in its own log shows it handling a password.
phases.cmd: kubectl logs -n banking-app -l app=banking-ui --tail=30

phases.step: Step 4 — Confirm personalized dashboard data
phases.does: The answer you get back is about you, and the numbers are yours.
phases.cmd: On /dashboard, click the **Show me my account balances** suggestion under the chat.
phases.expected: Balance figures specific to Oscar; the agent answers natural-language questions about Oscar's financial data.

phases.step: Step 5 — Switch users: sign in as Jaime
phases.does: Who signed in decides which money you see — two people, one app, no overlap.
phases.cmd: Open a **second Incognito / Private browser window** (this is your **jaime window**; the window you signed in to in Step 2 is your **oscar window**), go to the Banking UI URL, sign in as username `jaime` / password `WorkshopUser1!`, then click **Show me my account balances** again.
phases.expected: The agent answers with Jaime's accounts, not Oscar's. Keep both windows open; the pages that follow reuse them.

phases.step: Step 6 — Confirm the tool contract has nowhere to put an identity
phases.does: Nothing calling these tools can name which customer it wants to be, because there is no field to put a customer in.
phases.cmd:
kubectl delete pod mcp-probe -n banking-app --ignore-not-found --now >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl run mcp-probe --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -n banking-app \
  --command -- curl -s -X POST http://banking-mcp-svc:3001/mcp \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer schema-probe' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
    -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}' >/dev/null
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/mcp-probe -n banking-app --timeout=120s >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Failed pod/mcp-probe -n banking-app --timeout=30s >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl logs mcp-probe -n banking-app \
  | jq '.result.tools[] | {name, properties: .inputSchema.properties, required: .inputSchema.required}'
kubectl delete pod mcp-probe -n banking-app --now >/dev/null 2>&1
phases.expected: get_accounts: properties {} and required null; get_transactions: only an optional account_id, required null.

phases.step: Step 6 — Confirm the tool contract has nowhere to put an identity
phases.sub: Now prove it behaves that way
phases.does: The server really does act on the signed-in person's token from the request header and ignores any identity handed to it in the tool payload.
phases.cmd:
kubectl delete pod mcp-probe -n banking-app --ignore-not-found --now >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl run mcp-probe --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -n banking-app \
  --command -- curl -s -X POST http://banking-mcp-svc:3001/mcp \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer not-a-jwt-at-all' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
    -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_accounts",
         "arguments":{"jwt":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJvc2NhciJ9.not-a-real-signature"}}}' >/dev/null
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/mcp-probe -n banking-app --timeout=120s >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Failed pod/mcp-probe -n banking-app --timeout=30s >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl logs mcp-probe -n banking-app
kubectl delete pod mcp-probe -n banking-app --now >/dev/null 2>&1
phases.expected: Error fetching accounts: Invalid JWT format: expected header.payload.signature — isError true.

phases.step: Platform Track — IVIA OAuth client configuration
phases.sub: Confirm both properties on the running cluster
phases.does: The app's login secret never travels to your browser and is held in exactly one place on the server.
phases.cmd: kubectl get configmap -n banking-app banking-ui-config -o yaml | grep -c CLIENT_SECRET; kubectl get secret -n banking-app banking-ui-oidc -o jsonpath='{.data.IVIA_CLIENT_SECRET}' | wc -c
phases.expected: First number 0 (no CLIENT_SECRET in the ConfigMap); second number non-zero (the Secret holds it).

phases.step: Step 1 — Log in as Oscar, inspect accounts
phases.does: The app answers with your accounts and nobody else's.
phases.cmd: Switch to your **oscar window** (the one you signed in to on the OAuth Login Flow page) and, in the chat, ask "What are my account balances?" (or "show my accounts"). If you closed that window, open a new Incognito / Private window, go to the Banking UI URL, and log in as `oscar` as before.
phases.expected: Accounts belonging to Oscar only.

phases.step: Step 1 — Log in as Oscar, inspect accounts
phases.sub: Issue a credential of your own
phases.does: You hold a real, freshly minted database credential in your own hand, so the next check does not depend on the web app being honest.
phases.expected: The issued username and password printed as JSON; PG_USER, PG_PASS and RDS_HOST exported.

phases.step: Step 1 — Log in as Oscar, inspect accounts
phases.does: The narrowing to one customer's accounts happens inside the database itself, not in the web page you were looking at.
phases.cmd:
kubectl delete pod pg-client-oscar -n banking-app --ignore-not-found --now >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl run pg-client-oscar --restart=Never --image=postgres:16-alpine -n banking-app \
  --env="PGPASSWORD=${PG_PASS}" \
  --command -- psql -h "${RDS_HOST}" -U "${PG_USER}" -d workshop \
    -c "SET app.current_user_sub = 'oscar'; SELECT account_number, balance FROM banking.accounts;" >/dev/null
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/pg-client-oscar -n banking-app --timeout=120s >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Failed pod/pg-client-oscar -n banking-app --timeout=30s >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl logs pg-client-oscar -n banking-app
kubectl delete pod pg-client-oscar -n banking-app --now >/dev/null 2>&1
phases.expected: SET, then OVI-CHK-100001 4250.00 and OVI-SAV-100002 18750.50, (2 rows).

phases.step: Step 2 — Switch to Jaime, confirm data isolation
phases.does: Two customers using the same application never see each other's money.
phases.cmd: Switch to your **jaime window** (the second window from the OAuth Login Flow page). If you closed it, open a new Incognito / Private window, go to the Banking UI URL, and sign in as `jaime` (password `WorkshopUser1!`). In the chat, ask "What are my account balances?" (or "show my accounts").
phases.expected: Jaime's accounts only — no rows from Oscar's data.

phases.step: Step 2 — Switch to Jaime, confirm data isolation
phases.does: The separation follows the signed-in person, not the database login — the same credential returns a different customer's rows.
phases.cmd:
kubectl delete pod pg-client-jaime -n banking-app --ignore-not-found --now >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl run pg-client-jaime --restart=Never --image=postgres:16-alpine -n banking-app \
  --env="PGPASSWORD=${PG_PASS}" \
  --command -- psql -h "${RDS_HOST}" -U "${PG_USER}" -d workshop \
    -c "SET app.current_user_sub = 'jaime'; SELECT account_number, balance FROM banking.accounts;" >/dev/null
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/pg-client-jaime -n banking-app --timeout=120s >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Failed pod/pg-client-jaime -n banking-app --timeout=30s >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl logs pg-client-jaime -n banking-app
kubectl delete pod pg-client-jaime -n banking-app --now >/dev/null 2>&1

phases.step: Step 3 — Inspect the Row-Level Security policy
phases.does: There is one written rule in the database that made the two results differ — and if nobody says who is asking, it returns nothing rather than everything.
phases.cmd:
REGION=$(echo "${RDS_HOST}" | sed -E 's/.*\.([a-z0-9-]+)\.rds\.amazonaws\.com$/\1/')
SECRET_ARN=$(aws rds describe-db-instances --region "${REGION}" \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].MasterUserSecret.SecretArn' --output text)
SECRET_JSON=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --region "${REGION}" \
  --secret-id "${SECRET_ARN}" --query SecretString --output text)
MASTER_USER=$(echo "${SECRET_JSON}" | jq -r '.username')
MASTER_PASS=$(echo "${SECRET_JSON}" | jq -r '.password')

kubectl create secret generic db-master -n banking-app \
  --from-literal=password="${MASTER_PASS}" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

kubectl delete pod pg-client-policy -n banking-app --ignore-not-found --now >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl run pg-client-policy --restart=Never --image=postgres:16-alpine -n banking-app \
  --overrides="$(jq -n --arg host "${RDS_HOST}" --arg user "${MASTER_USER}" \
    --arg sql "SELECT polname, polcmd, polroles, pg_get_expr(polqual, polrelid) AS policy_expr FROM pg_policy JOIN pg_class ON pg_class.oid = pg_policy.polrelid WHERE pg_class.relname = 'accounts';" \
    '{spec:{containers:[{name:"pg-client-policy",image:"postgres:16-alpine",env:[{name:"PGPASSWORD",valueFrom:{secretKeyRef:{name:"db-master",key:"password"}}}],command:["psql","-h",$host,"-U",$user,"-d","workshop","-c",$sql]}],restartPolicy:"Never"}}')" >/dev/null
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/pg-client-policy -n banking-app --timeout=120s >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Failed pod/pg-client-policy -n banking-app --timeout=30s >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl logs pg-client-policy -n banking-app
kubectl delete pod pg-client-policy -n banking-app --now >/dev/null 2>&1

kubectl delete secret db-master -n banking-app
phases.expected: secret/db-master created; one row — user_accounts | r | {0} | ((user_sub)::text = current_setting('app.current_user_sub'::text, true)); then secret deleted.

phases.step: Step 4 — Run verify-uc2.sh
phases.does: Every promise this use case makes — read-only, per-person, blocked outbound traffic, no identity in the tool arguments, a live lease — checks out in one command.
phases.cmd: bash infrastructure/scripts/verify-uc2.sh
phases.expected: 21 check(s) passed.

phases.does: You are inspecting the credential and lease paths as the operator — which is exactly why the agent itself cannot reach them.
phases.cmd: export VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN=$(jq -r '.root_token' ~/vault-init.json)

phases.step: Step 1 — Issue a fresh credential and capture the lease_id
phases.does: You have one specific credential and its receipt number, which you can now follow through the database, through Vault, and into the audit trail.
phases.expected: LEASE_ID=database/creds/uc2-personal-readonly/<id> and PG_USER=v-root-uc2-pers-<random>-<timestamp>.

phases.step: Step 2 — Confirm the Postgres role exists
phases.does: The credential is a real database login that exists right now — so its disappearance later will mean something.
phases.cmd:
RDS_HOST=$(kubectl get configmap banking-mcp-config -n banking-app -o jsonpath='{.data.RDS_ADDRESS}')
REGION=$(echo "${RDS_HOST}" | sed -E 's/.*\.([a-z0-9-]+)\.rds\.amazonaws\.com$/\1/')
SECRET_ARN=$(aws rds describe-db-instances --region "${REGION}" \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].MasterUserSecret.SecretArn' --output text)
SECRET_JSON=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --region "${REGION}" \
  --secret-id "${SECRET_ARN}" --query SecretString --output text)
MASTER_USER=$(echo "${SECRET_JSON}" | jq -r '.username')
MASTER_PASS=$(echo "${SECRET_JSON}" | jq -r '.password')

kubectl create secret generic db-master -n banking-app \
  --from-literal=password="${MASTER_PASS}" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

kubectl delete pod pg-role-before -n banking-app --ignore-not-found --now >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl run pg-role-before --restart=Never --image=postgres:16-alpine -n banking-app \
  --overrides="$(jq -n --arg host "${RDS_HOST}" --arg user "${MASTER_USER}" \
    --arg sql "SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='${PG_USER}';" \
    '{spec:{containers:[{name:"pg-role-before",image:"postgres:16-alpine",env:[{name:"PGPASSWORD",valueFrom:{secretKeyRef:{name:"db-master",key:"password"}}}],command:["psql","-h",$host,"-U",$user,"-d","workshop","-c",$sql]}],restartPolicy:"Never"}}')" >/dev/null
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/pg-role-before -n banking-app --timeout=120s >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Failed pod/pg-role-before -n banking-app --timeout=30s >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl logs pg-role-before -n banking-app
kubectl delete pod pg-role-before -n banking-app --now >/dev/null 2>&1
phases.expected: secret/db-master created; exactly one row — the fresh v-root-uc2-pers-… rolname.

phases.step: Step 3 — Revoke the lease (the production code path)
phases.does: Handing a credential back is a single call — the same one the application makes for itself the moment a query finishes.
phases.cmd:
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- \
  sh -c "VAULT_TOKEN='${VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN}' vault lease revoke '${LEASE_ID}'"
phases.expected: All revocation operations queued successfully!

phases.step: Step 4 — Confirm the Postgres role is gone
phases.does: Once handed back, the database login no longer exists at all — the access it granted is impossible rather than merely expired.
phases.cmd:
kubectl delete pod pg-role-after -n banking-app --ignore-not-found --now >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl run pg-role-after --restart=Never --image=postgres:16-alpine -n banking-app \
  --overrides="$(jq -n --arg host "${RDS_HOST}" --arg user "${MASTER_USER}" \
    --arg sql "SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='${PG_USER}';" \
    '{spec:{containers:[{name:"pg-role-after",image:"postgres:16-alpine",env:[{name:"PGPASSWORD",valueFrom:{secretKeyRef:{name:"db-master",key:"password"}}}],command:["psql","-h",$host,"-U",$user,"-d","workshop","-c",$sql]}],restartPolicy:"Never"}}')" >/dev/null
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/pg-role-after -n banking-app --timeout=120s >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Failed pod/pg-role-after -n banking-app --timeout=30s >/dev/null 2>&1
kubectl logs pg-role-after -n banking-app
kubectl delete pod pg-role-after -n banking-app --now >/dev/null 2>&1

kubectl delete secret db-master -n banking-app
phases.expected: (0 rows), then secret "db-master" deleted.

phases.step: Step 5 — Confirm your lease is no longer in Vault's active-leases list
phases.does: Vault's own list of credentials it still considers live agrees with the database — the two have not drifted apart.
phases.cmd:
LEASE_SUFFIX=${LEASE_ID##*/}

kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- \
  sh -c "VAULT_TOKEN='${VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN}' \
  vault list sys/leases/lookup/database/creds/uc2-personal-readonly" 2>&1 \
  | grep -F "${LEASE_SUFFIX}" \
  && echo "FAIL: lease ${LEASE_SUFFIX} is still active" \
  || echo "PASS: lease ${LEASE_SUFFIX} is no longer in the active-leases list"
phases.expected: PASS: lease <suffix> is no longer in the active-leases list.

phases.step: Step 5 — Confirm your lease is no longer in Vault's active-leases list
phases.sub: What does the raw listing look like?
phases.does: You can read the unfiltered list of live credentials yourself instead of trusting the PASS line above it.
phases.cmd:
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- \
  sh -c "VAULT_TOKEN='${VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN}' \
  vault list sys/leases/lookup/database/creds/uc2-personal-readonly" 2>&1
phases.expected: Either "No value found at sys/leases/lookup/database/creds/uc2-personal-readonly" with exit code 2, or a Keys table of other live lease suffixes — never yours.

phases.step: Step 6 — Find the issuance event in the audit log (Athena)
phases.does: You can put questions to the audit trail from your own shell, against your own deployment's region.
phases.cmd:
# The Glue catalog + Athena 'workshop' workgroup were provisioned in YOUR deploy
# region. Resolve it from the RDS endpoint (kubectl-sourced, so it works regardless
# of your shell's default region or working directory) — never a hardcoded literal,
# per the region contract.
RDS_HOST=$(kubectl get configmap banking-mcp-config -n banking-app -o jsonpath='{.data.RDS_ADDRESS}')
export AWS_REGION=$(echo "${RDS_HOST}" | sed -E 's/.*\.([a-z0-9-]+)\.rds\.amazonaws\.com$/\1/')

athena_query() {
  local Q="$1"
  local QID=$(aws athena start-query-execution --work-group workshop \
    --query-string "$Q" --query 'QueryExecutionId' --output text)
  for i in $(seq 1 30); do
    STATE=$(aws athena get-query-execution --query-execution-id "$QID" \
      --query 'QueryExecution.Status.State' --output text)
    [ "$STATE" = "SUCCEEDED" ] && break
    [ "$STATE" = "FAILED" ] && { aws athena get-query-execution \
      --query-execution-id "$QID" --query 'QueryExecution.Status.StateChangeReason' --output text; return 1; }
    sleep 2
  done
  aws athena get-query-results --query-execution-id "$QID" --output json \
    | jq -r '.ResultSet.Rows[] | [.Data[] | (.VarCharValue // "" | if . == "" then "-" else . end)] | @tsv' \
    | column -t -s $'\t'
}

# First value of the first data row only (capture into a variable; empty if none)
athena_scalar() { athena_query "$1" | awk 'NR==2 {print ($1=="-" ? "" : $1)}'; }

phases.step: Step 6 — Find the issuance event in the audit log (Athena)
phases.does: Every credential handed out names both the person it was for and the agent that asked — recorded whether or not anyone ever goes looking.
phases.cmd:
athena_query "SELECT
  substr(timestamp, 1, 19) AS time,
  auth.display_name AS identity,
  auth.metadata['actor_entity_name'] AS agent,
  auth.entity_id AS human_entity
FROM workshop_logs.vault_audit
WHERE type = 'response'
  AND request.path = 'database/creds/uc2-personal-readonly'
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 10;"
phases.expected: Rows with identity=root and agent "-" for hand-issued reads, and identity="JWT Token with Unique Identifier: <jti>" with agent=agent-uc2 plus a human_entity id for signed-in queries.

phases.step: Step 6 — Find the issuance event in the audit log (Athena)
phases.does: The identifier in the audit row is read from Vault's own audit record and resolves to a named person, so the record reads as a human rather than a hash.
phases.cmd:
# Most recent issuance that carries a human entity (skips the root rows)
HUMAN_ENTITY=$(athena_scalar "SELECT auth.entity_id
FROM workshop_logs.vault_audit
WHERE type = 'response'
  AND request.path = 'database/creds/uc2-personal-readonly'
  AND auth.entity_id IS NOT NULL AND auth.entity_id <> ''
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 1")
echo "human_entity: ${HUMAN_ENTITY}"

kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- \
  sh -c "VAULT_TOKEN='${VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN}' vault read -format=json identity/entity/id/${HUMAN_ENTITY}" \
  | jq '{id: .data.id, name: .data.name}'

phases.step: Step 8 — Watch the MCP server hand a credential back on its own
phases.does: The credential the application used really is gone, while the ones you minted by hand are still sitting there — the contrast is the point.

    | grep -F "${LEASE_SUFFIX}" \

    || echo "PASS: lease ${LEASE_SUFFIX} is no longer in the active-leases list"
fi

phases.step: Set up the query helpers
phases.does: The rest of the page reads as one command per question, pointed at the log catalog in your own deploy region.
phases.cmd:
# The Glue catalog + Athena 'workshop' workgroup were provisioned in YOUR deploy
# region (resolved from Terraform state — never a hardcoded literal, per the region
# contract). Point the CLI at that region so the workgroup and the workshop_logs
# database resolve regardless of your shell's default region.
export AWS_REGION="$(terraform -chdir=infrastructure output -raw region)"

# Run a query in the 'workshop' workgroup, wait for it, echo the execution id
athena_run() {
  local QID=$(aws athena start-query-execution --work-group workshop \
    --query-string "$1" --query 'QueryExecutionId' --output text)
  for i in $(seq 1 30); do
    local S=$(aws athena get-query-execution --query-execution-id "$QID" \
      --query 'QueryExecution.Status.State' --output text)
    [ "$S" = "SUCCEEDED" ] && { echo "$QID"; return 0; }
    [ "$S" = "FAILED" ] && { aws athena get-query-execution --query-execution-id "$QID" \
      --query 'QueryExecution.Status.StateChangeReason' --output text >&2; return 1; }
    sleep 2
  done
}

# Multi-row aligned table
athena_query() { aws athena get-query-results --query-execution-id "$(athena_run "$1")" \
  --output json | jq -r '.ResultSet.Rows[] | [.Data[] | (.VarCharValue // "-")] | @tsv' | column -t -s $'\t'; }

# Single row, vertical (field -> value)
athena_record() { aws athena get-query-results --query-execution-id "$(athena_run "$1")" \
  --output json | jq -r '.ResultSet.Rows as $r | range(0; ($r[0].Data|length)) as $i
    | "\($r[0].Data[$i].VarCharValue)\t\($r[1].Data[$i].VarCharValue // "-")"' | column -t -s $'\t'; }

# First value only (capture into a variable)
athena_scalar() { aws athena get-query-results --query-execution-id "$(athena_run "$1")" \
  --query 'ResultSet.Rows[1].Data[0].VarCharValue' --output text; }

echo "tracing: ${REQUEST_ID}"

  auth.entity_id                                  AS human_entity,
  auth.metadata['actor_entity_name']              AS agent,
  auth.metadata['jwt_audience_claim']             AS audience,

phases.step: Read the Vault record yourself
phases.sub: Resolve the human entity to a name
phases.does: The opaque id in the log is read from the same Vault audit record and resolves to the person who tapped Approve on their phone — the audit trail names the human, not just the software.
phases.cmd:
export VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN=$(jq -r '.root_token' ~/vault-init.json)

# Capture the entity id from the same Vault audit record you just read
HUMAN_ENTITY=$(athena_scalar "SELECT auth.entity_id
FROM workshop_logs.vault_audit
WHERE type = 'response'
  AND request.path = 'database/creds/uc3-refund-writer'
  AND (error IS NULL OR error = '')
  AND element_at(element_at(request.headers, 'x-correlation-id'), 1) = '${REQUEST_ID}'
LIMIT 1")

# An empty result or "None" means the audit row has not landed yet
if [ -z "${HUMAN_ENTITY}" ] || [ "${HUMAN_ENTITY}" = "None" ]; then
  echo "The audit row has not landed yet. Wait about a minute and run this step again."
else
  echo "human_entity: ${HUMAN_ENTITY}"
  kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- \
    sh -c "VAULT_TOKEN='${VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN}' vault read -format=json identity/entity/id/${HUMAN_ENTITY}" \
    | jq '{id: .data.id, name: .data.name}'
fi
phases.expected: A JSON object with the id and the name of the approver, for example jaime.

phases.step: How the approved amount is proven — consent-bound by correlation
phases.sub: Read the refund amount from Postgres
phases.does: The dollar figure the person approved is read straight from the refund row under the same request_id, so the amount is shown rather than assumed.
phases.cmd:
OWNER=$(athena_scalar "SELECT user_approved_sub FROM workshop_logs.audit_correlation
  WHERE request_id = '${REQUEST_ID}' LIMIT 1")

# An empty result or "None" means the audit row has not landed yet
if [ -z "${OWNER}" ] || [ "${OWNER}" = "None" ]; then
  echo "The audit row has not landed yet. Wait about a minute and run this step again."
else
  export VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN=$(jq -r '.root_token' ~/vault-init.json)
  CREDS_JSON=$(kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- \
    sh -c "VAULT_TOKEN='${VAULT_ROOT_TOKEN}' vault read database/creds/uc3-readonly -format=json")
  PG_USER=$(echo "$CREDS_JSON" | jq -r '.data.username')
  PG_PASS=$(echo "$CREDS_JSON" | jq -r '.data.password')
  RDS_HOST=$(kubectl get configmap uc3-agent-config -n banking-app -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_HOST}')

  kubectl delete pod pg-refund-amount -n banking-app --ignore-not-found --now >/dev/null 2>&1
  kubectl run pg-refund-amount --restart=Never --image=postgres:16-alpine -n banking-app \
    --env="PGPASSWORD=${PG_PASS}" \
    --command -- psql -h "${RDS_HOST}" -U "${PG_USER}" -d workshop -c "
      SELECT set_config('app.current_user_sub','${OWNER}',false);
      SELECT request_id, refund_id, account_id, transaction_id, amount, currency, approved_by, created_at
        FROM banking.refunds WHERE request_id = '${REQUEST_ID}';" >/dev/null
  kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/pg-refund-amount -n banking-app --timeout=120s >/dev/null 2>&1 \
    || kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Failed pod/pg-refund-amount -n banking-app --timeout=30s >/dev/null 2>&1
  kubectl logs pg-refund-amount -n banking-app
  kubectl delete pod pg-refund-amount -n banking-app --now >/dev/null 2>&1
fi
phases.expected: Exactly one row under the request_id you are tracing; its amount is the figure the user approved.
